A1.justification: Both complete PDFs describe the same ClinEdu simulator, ClinTeach dataset, and tutor, renamed from MedTutor-R1 to ClinTutor-R1. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation and medical VQA evaluations, ablations, scalability tests, expert ratings, and a real-user study.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports expanded human studies, judge-robustness results, and controlled error-correction experiments.

M1.justification: The structured thinking tags, agent interaction and review procedures, SFT followed by GRPO, and three-axis reward with a safety veto are retained. The Theory-of-Mind terminology and reward-hacking discussion do not establish a new method component; corresponding appendix prompts remain substantively unchanged.

E1.justification: The existing clinical and VQA benchmarks remain. v2 adds controlled scenarios involving factual errors, premature diagnostic closure, and safety or ethical risks, and explicitly broadens human participants from undergraduates to a cohort spanning junior students through senior interns.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain their comparator sets, and new analyses reuse existing tutor baselines. The setup's o1-to-o3 edit matches o3 already reported in v1's tables. Gemini 3 Pro and GPT-5 are additional judges, not competing tutors.

E3.justification: Expert evaluation expands from 50 to 100 dialogues, and the user study from three to 200 participants. New protocols re-score 100 cases using three judges and manually evaluate immediate next-turn error correction across 300 cases with four-student groups. Existing training settings and benchmark splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds judge-sensitivity testing, controlled misconception-correction experiments, and analysis of reward-hacking behaviors and veto activation during training. These address evaluator dependence and remediation effectiveness beyond the retained component ablations, student-model robustness tests, and scalability analysis.

E5.justification: Section 5.3 newly reports statistical significance against the strongest expert-evaluation baseline at p < 0.05, without specifying the test. Three-run means and standard deviations, and the reported agreement value of 0.79, were already present in v1.

E6.justification: Table 4 replaces human ratings under expanded samples, including the tutor's reported expert average changing from 8.64 to 8.73; this is not a same-setting gain. New results include cross-judge scores, 88.50% correction success versus GPT-4o's 81.53%, and declining veto activation. Main benchmark, ablation, and existing robustness scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The reward, veto, and GRPO equations are retained, with no new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs. The added correction-success measure applies the standard corrected/total success-rate formula as an empirical evaluation metric.

C1.justification: The central simulator, dataset, one-to-many tutor, and relative-performance claims persist. v2 recasts the contribution around Theory-of-Mind-based alignment and adds a concrete claim of sub-five-second latency with up to ten students, extending its practical scalability claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of reward hacking, safeguards, error remediation, and possible rubric transfer beyond medicine. New limitations address simulation realism, static-image-only perception, unmeasured long-term learning, and increasing latency, while explicitly restricting applicability to educational simulation.

D1.justification: A new reproducibility statement documents a commitment to release the full code and dataset. The setup explicitly identifies LLaVA as another backbone, whose variant already appeared in v1. Training hyperparameters, hardware, durations, and operational prompts are otherwise retained; the release commitment does not establish actual availability.

R1.justification: The research positioning shifts substantially toward limitations of dyadic alignment, pluralistic objectives, Theory of Mind, and context dilution. New references include Ouyang et al., Sorensen et al., and Rabinowitz et al.; related-work discussions sharpen distinctions from single-student, non-clinical tutoring systems.

P1.justification: The title and tutor name change, the abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and method descriptions are compressed. Related work is reordered and revised, while reproducibility, ethics, limitations, and additional appendix sections reorganize the narrative. Most existing appendix prompts receive only punctuation edits.

P2.justification: The new opening Figure 1 combines alignment schematics with a redrawn version of the earlier scalability plot. v2 adds the judge-comparison table and error-correction chart, moves Algorithm 1 into the appendix, and rearranges existing displays. Most established figures and table structures are retained.

improvement.justification: The broader human evaluation, independent-judge checks, and controlled misconception tests substantially address v1's weak real-user validation and limited testing of evaluator dependence and correction effectiveness. Explicit limitations also improve claim calibration. These gains outweigh reporting shortcomings: Figure 5 remains unchanged despite revised Table 4 scores, and the new significance and latency claims lack supporting test or timing details.
